description: I'm Sabekun Nahar Shefa, a CSE student at the University of Asia Pacific (UAP). Our team consists of passionate CSE students interested in gaming, AI, and software development. We aim to build an innovative space mission game for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. We welcome members skilled in game development, AI, UI/UX design, and space science.

details:
What it does

PARADOX Space Academy is a web game that turns real NASA data into space missions for kids. We built it because most children love space, but in class it often becomes a page of facts and the same quiz again and again. We wanted them to explore it instead of memorizing it.

How it works

You start by picking a planet and a level. Easy gives you three answer options, while Medium and Hard give you four and make you think a bit harder. Each mission begins with something going wrong, and you fix it by answering science questions and making decisions along the way.

All the questions come from real NASA data. Some we wrote and checked ourselves, and others are calculated straight from NASA's Planetary Fact Sheet, like how long a year lasts on Mars or how much you'd weigh on Jupiter. The game also remembers every question you've answered, so you never see the same one twice. Each student gets more than 400 fresh questions.

If you get stuck, you can ask Zippy, our AI co-pilot. Zippy explains the answer in simple words, in English or Bangla, and shows which NASA sources it used. Even without an AI key, it still answers from our checked NASA fact sheets instead of making things up.

There's more to explore too: story missions where your choices change the ending, a Solar Storm challenge built on NASA's DONKI space-weather data, and a Mission Control Data Desk with NASA's picture of the day and real asteroid data. Kids can sing along to space songs or play bonus mini-games like Planet Smash, Cosmic Quiz and Planet Weight Lab. We also added a Space Energy bar. When a child has been learning for a while and starts getting tired, it suggests a quick "smash a planet" break, and then they're back to learning. Parents can check their child's progress in a password-protected Parent Zone.

Why it matters

Lots of children, especially in schools without telescopes or science labs, never get to experience space science as something exciting. PARADOX runs in a normal web browser, so it works on a phone, tablet or laptop. Even a family with one shared phone can use it. Next, we want to test it in real classrooms in Dhaka, add a full Bangla voice for kids who can't read yet, and build an offline mode for places with weak internet.

How we built it

The frontend uses React, Vite, Tailwind CSS and Three.js, and the backend runs on Python with FastAPI and SQLite. Zippy and our question generator use the OpenAI API. Our data comes from NASA's Planetary Fact Sheet, DONKI, APOD, NeoWs and NASA Science pages. The live version is hosted on Render with Docker. We used Claude as a coding assistant, and ChatGPT only to help polish our prompts.

What makes it creative

We took tables full of NASA numbers and turned them into puzzles kids actually want to solve, and every answer can be traced back to where it came from. We also believe feelings are part of learning. When a child is frustrated, they can smash a cartoon planet, watch it rebuild itself with a smile, and then happily get back to their mission.

What we kept in mind

Children's safety came first, so Zippy only gives educational, age-appropriate answers, and our API keys stay safely on the server. We made sure every question has exactly one correct answer backed by NASA data. For accessibility, we never rely on color alone, and we added read-aloud, reduced motion, and keyboard and touch controls. Most of all, we kept it free and light so it can run on low-cost devices.
